An application check does see rows other requests have already committed; what it cannot see is an insert still in flight, which is exactly the window the constraint covers. Dropping the extra SELECT is a side benefit, not the reason, and you still have to catch the duplicate error and turn it into a usable message.

fields.explanation: SERIALIZABLE is the strongest of the four standard levels: concurrent transactions must produce a result that some serial order of them would have produced, so no standard anomaly is possible. The strength is not free: PostgreSQL enforces it by aborting transactions with a serialization failure, SQLSTATE 40001, so any application running at this level has to retry the whole transaction.

fields.explanation: OFFSET does not skip work: the server still computes the skipped rows in order and throws them away, so page 1000 costs roughly a thousand times page 1. Sorting is not the part that grows, because the same ORDER BY costs the same whether you ask for page 1 or page 1000, while the rows produced and discarded grow with the offset. Keyset (seek) pagination replaces it with WHERE (created_at, id) < (last_seen_values) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT n, which starts at the right place in the index and stays flat as the page number grows. What you give up is arbitrary jumps: keyset moves forward and back from a known row, not straight to page 500, and it needs a sort key that is unique and stable.

problems: hint states the key almost verbatim ('can the database reach row 100001 without producing the hundred thousand before it')
option 0 is partly true and unrefuted: each page request does re-run the query and re-sort when no index supplies the order, so the explanation has to say why that is not what grows with the offset
evidence: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-limit.html : 'The rows skipped by an OFFSET clause still have to be computed inside the server; therefore a large OFFSET might be inefficient.'

https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-limit.html : 'When using LIMIT, it is important to use an ORDER BY clause that constrains the result rows into a unique order', which is the stable-key requirement the keyset caveat names
notes: Keyset pagination keeps its stated cost (no jump to an arbitrary page, unique stable sort key), so it is not presented as a free win.

evidence: knowledge: EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports per-node actual time and row counts against the planner's estimates, which is what locates the cost
knowledge: each distractor carries the cost the explanation gives it: indexes slow writes, a cache hides a degrading query, and a replica adds lag
notes: Hint gives the situation rather than naming an option, and every premature fix is priced, which closes the level honestly.
